DOCUMENT:
Post-mortem: Larder App v5.0 Navigation Redesign
Product team, 20 March 2026 (blameless format)

Summary
On 2 February 2026 we released v5.0 of the Larder grocery app on iOS and Android, replacing the five-tab bottom navigation with a three-tab layout and a persistent search bar. Weekly orders fell sharply in the following weeks. We identified the removal of the Reorder button from the home screen as the main cause and restored it in v5.0.3 on 2 March, after which orders recovered to close to pre-release levels. This document sets out what happened, what we learned and what we will change.

What changed in v5.0
- Bottom navigation reduced from five tabs (Home, Browse, Search, Orders, Account) to three (Home, Browse, Account), with search moved to a persistent bar at the top of every screen.
- The Reorder button, which let customers repeat a previous order with one tap from the home screen, moved into Account > Order history.
- A new recipe-led home feed.
The release passed our standard usability testing with 12 participants, all of whom were new users recruited through a research panel. No existing customers were included.

Impact
Table 1. Weekly active users (WAU) and orders
Week starting | WAU | Orders | Orders per WAU
19 Jan | 48,200 | 61,700 | 1.28
26 Jan | 48,600 | 62,200 | 1.28
2 Feb (v5.0 released) | 47,900 | 55,100 | 1.15
9 Feb | 46,800 | 51,500 | 1.10
16 Feb | 46,300 | 50,900 | 1.10
23 Feb | 46,100 | 50,700 | 1.10
2 Mar (v5.0.3, Reorder restored) | 46,400 | 56,600 | 1.22
9 Mar | 47,000 | 59,700 | 1.27

Between the two pre-release weeks (average 61,950 orders) and the three weeks from 9 to 23 February (average about 51,030), weekly orders fell by about 10,900, or 18%. Orders per active user fell from 1.28 to 1.10, while WAU fell only about 4%, which told us that customers were still opening the app but not completing orders.

Across the four weeks from 2 to 23 February, we estimate that 39,600 orders were lost relative to the pre-release baseline. At our average order value of £38, this is approximately £1.05 million in lost revenue.

Table 2. Change in weekly orders by platform, pre-release vs 9-23 February
Platform | Share of WAU | Change in orders
iOS | 58% | -21%
Android | 42% | -13%

The decline was concentrated among Android users, which is consistent with the Android build placing order history one level deeper in the Account menu than the iOS build does.

Root cause
Session recordings and support tickets both pointed to the Reorder button. Support contacts mentioning "reorder", "repeat order" or "last order" rose from about 40 a week to 410 in the week of 9 February. Roughly 45% of pre-release orders had been placed through Reorder, and the new path to it required four taps instead of one. When v5.0.3 restored the button to the home screen on 2 March, orders per user recovered to 1.22 that week and 1.27 the following week, close to the pre-release 1.28. The timing of both the fall and the recovery, and the absence of any other change in v5.0.3, make us confident in this diagnosis.

Detection
The drop was visible in the daily orders dashboard on 3 February, but nobody was watching orders per user as a release metric, and the first escalation came on 10 February. The rollback decision was then delayed while we prepared a fix rather than reverting.

What went well
The persistent search bar has been a success. Customers who used the new search bar at least once in a week placed 40% more orders that week than customers who did not. Search is clearly driving purchasing, and we will build on this by making search results the default landing view for returning users in v5.2.

What we will change
1. Usability tests for changes to existing flows will include at least six existing customers, weighted towards frequent buyers.
2. Any release that moves an element used in more than 10% of orders will be staged to 10% of users for a week, with orders per WAU as a guardrail metric.
3. An automated alert will fire when orders per WAU falls more than 5% week on week.
4. For regressions in core purchase flows, the default response will be to revert first and fix afterwards.

Conclusion
The incident was caused by moving a heavily used shortcut without testing with the customers who relied on it, and was prolonged by weak release monitoring. Both are fixable, and the actions above address them directly.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "At our average order value of £38, this is approximately £1.05 million in lost revenue." -- 39,600 lost orders x £38 = £1,504,800, i.e. about £1.5 million, not £1.05 million. (The 39,600 itself is correct: 6,850 + 10,450 + 11,050 + 11,250.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "The decline was concentrated among Android users, which is consistent with the Android build placing order history one level deeper" -- Table 2 shows orders fell 21% on iOS and only 13% on Android, so the decline was concentrated on iOS, not Android. The text inverts the table and builds an explanation on the misreading.
3. [unsupported_causal] at: "Search is clearly driving purchasing, and we will build on this by making search results the default landing view" -- The evidence is a correlation between using search and ordering more in the same week. More engaged/frequent buyers (or customers already intending to buy) are more likely to use search, so selection and reverse causation explain the association; it does not show search drives purchasing.

REVIEW:
# Review: not ready to send yet

The diagnosis is sound, but two figures contradict the document's own data, one conclusion isn't supported, and the asks lack owners and dates.

## Errors to fix before sending

**1. The revenue figure is wrong.** 39,600 orders × £38 = **£1,504,800, about £1.5 million**, not £1.05 million. The order count checks out (61,950 × 4 = 247,800 baseline, minus 208,200 actual = 39,600), so the revenue line is the error. It understates the cost by about £450k, which matters when leadership is weighing the investment in the fixes.

The estimate is also conservative. It stops at 23 February, but the weeks of 2 March (56,600) and 9 March (59,700) were still below baseline by roughly 7,600 orders combined, or about £290k more. Either extend the window or say explicitly that the figure excludes the recovery weeks.

**2. The platform finding is backwards.** Table 2 shows iOS fell 21% and Android 13%, yet the text says the decline "was concentrated among Android users" and ties it to Android's deeper menu. The data shows the opposite, and the weighted average (0.58×21 + 0.42×13 ≈ 17.6%) matches the overall 18%, so the table looks internally consistent. Either the table labels are swapped, or the narrative is wrong and the Android menu explanation has no support. Check the source data. If iOS really was hit harder, the explanation has to be removed or replaced, and the "target the fix" argument disappears.

## Unsupported conclusion

**3. "Search is clearly driving purchasing" is a correlation.** Customers who use search at least once a week are probably heavier, more engaged buyers anyway, so the 40% gap says little about the effect of the search bar. Search was also a dedicated tab before v5.0, so there's no before/after comparison. This claim is the sole basis for making search results the default landing view for returning users in v5.2.

That plan also repeats the failure mode the post-mortem describes: changing the entry flow for existing customers, 45% of whom were reordering. Either drop it from this document, or present it as a hypothesis to test under the new staged-rollout rules (action 2).

## Gaps for decision-makers

**4. No explicit recommendation or ask.** The document ends with "the actions above address them directly" but doesn't say what you need from the readers: approval, resourcing, or just acknowledgement. Add a short "Decisions requested" section.

**5. The actions are not yet owned or dated.** The author describes them as "concrete, owned and measurable," but the list has no owners, deadlines or success measures. Add those for each action. Action 4 ("revert first") also needs a defined trigger, such as the alert threshold plus who can authorise the revert.

**6. Smaller points:**
- The natural-experiment argument is strong for Reorder, but the document should say that other v5.0 changes (the recipe feed, the tab reduction) were not isolated. Recovery to 1.27 vs 1.28 suggests they were roughly neutral, and it's worth stating that explicitly.
- The restored Reorder button returned orders per user to 1.27 vs 1.28 pre-release. Say whether you expect the last gap to close.
- The detection section would be stronger with a simple timeline: drop visible on 3 Feb, escalated on 10 Feb, fix shipped on 2 March, so the response took 4 weeks.

## What is solid
The table arithmetic (orders per WAU, the 18% drop, the 4% WAU decline) all checks out. The support-contact rise (40 to 410) and the timing of the fall and recovery make a convincing case for the Reorder diagnosis. The testing and monitoring gaps are correctly identified.

Once the revenue figure and platform finding are corrected, the search claim is softened, and the actions have owners and dates, this will be ready to go.
